subtopics.name: Key points
points: Angular displacement is measured in radians; 2π rad = 360° = 1 revolution.
Angular velocity is a vector along the axis (right-hand rule), not tangential.
The kinematic equations for rotation mirror linear motion: x→θ, v→ω, a→α.
v = rω links linear and angular speed — the basis of all circular motion problems.
Always convert rpm to rad/s before using formulas: multiply by 2π/60.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Angular velocity: ω = dθ/dt (instantaneous), ω = Δθ/t (average)
Angular acceleration: α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt²
Kinematic equations (constant α): ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ
Linear-angular links: v = rω; a_t = rα; a_c = v²/r = rω²
rpm conversion: ω (rad/s) = rpm × 2π/60; revolutions = θ/(2π)

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: rpm to rad/s conversion is tested every year — know the factor 2π/60.
Kinematic equation problems (constant α) are standard — practice all four equations.
Linear-angular link problems (v = rω, a = rω²) are common — know both formulas.
rpm shortcut: multiply by 2π/60 to get rad/s — memorize this conversion factor.
Revolutions shortcut: divide θ (in radians) by 2π — no conversion needed.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Centripetal force is NOT a new force — it is the resultant of real forces (tension, gravity, friction).
Centripetal acceleration changes only the direction of velocity, not its magnitude.
Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force that appears only in rotating reference frames.
If the centripetal force is removed, the body moves tangent to the circle.
Centripetal force is proportional to v² — doubling speed quadruples the required force.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Centripetal acceleration: $a_c = v^2/r = r\omega^2$ (directed toward the centre)
Centripetal force: $F_c = mv^2/r = mr\omega^2$ (resultant of real forces toward centre)
Maximum speed (string): $v_{max} = \sqrt{T_{max} \times r/m}$ — when tension reaches breaking point
Maximum speed (flat curve): $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s rg}$ — when friction reaches its maximum
Cyclist lean angle: $\tan \theta = v^2/(rg)$ — the angle needed to balance torque

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the centre of the circular path: a_c = v²/r = rω².
Centripetal force is the resultant of real forces pointing toward the centre — it is not a new force.
If the centripetal force is removed, the body moves tangent to the circle (Newton's first law).

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: Maximum-speed problems (string breaking, car skidding) are the most common type.
Always identify which real force provides the centripetal force — never add it as a separate force.
Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force — use it only in rotating reference frames.
Force identification trick: always ask 'which real force points toward the centre?' — that's your F_c.
Maximum speed shortcut: v_max = √(μ_s rg) for flat curves, v_max = √(T_max r/m) for strings.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: The period of a conical pendulum depends only on L cos θ (the vertical height of the cone), not on mass.
The faster the rotation, the larger the angle θ — the cone becomes flatter.
The minimum period (θ → 0) equals the period of a simple pendulum of the same length.
The tension is always greater than mg: T = mg/cos θ.
The centripetal force is the horizontal component of tension — no new force is added.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Vertical equilibrium: $T \cos \theta = mg$
Centripetal force: $T \sin \theta = m\omega^2 L \sin \theta ightarrow T = m\omega^2 L$
Angular speed: $\omega = \sqrt{g/(L \cos \theta)}$
Period: $T_{period} = 2\pi\sqrt{L \cos \theta/g}$ — independent of mass
Radius of circle: $r = L \sin \theta$

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: The period of a conical pendulum (T = 2π√(L cos θ/g)) is independent of the mass of the bob.
The centripetal force is provided by the horizontal component of tension: T sin θ = mω²r.
The vertical component of tension balances the weight: T cos θ = mg.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: The derivation of cos θ = g/(ω²L) is the most common NEB question on this topic.
Period problems: use T = 2π√(L cos θ/g) — know this formula.
Tension problems: use T = mg/cos θ — remember T > mg.
Period shortcut: T = 2π√(L cos θ/g) — just plug in L cos θ and g.
Angular speed shortcut: ω = √(g/L cos θ) — the square root of g over L cos θ.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: The minimum speed at the top (string) is √(gr), independent of mass.
The minimum speed at the bottom (string) is √(5gr) — the most tested result.
For a rigid rod, v_bottom(min) = √(2gr) — the rod can push, not just pull.
Tension at the bottom is always maximum; at the top it is minimum.
At the minimum case (string), T_bottom = 6mg — six times the weight.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Minimum speed at top (string): v_top = √(gr)
Minimum speed at bottom (string): v_bottom = √(5gr)
Minimum speed at bottom (rod): v_bottom = √(2gr)
Tension at bottom: T_bottom = mg + mv²/r
Tension at top: T_top = mv²/r − mg

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: The minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle (string) is √(gr), independent of mass.
The minimum speed at the bottom (string) is √(5gr) — derived from energy conservation.
For a rigid rod, the body can complete the circle with v_top = 0, giving v_bottom(min) = √(2gr).

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: √(5gr) is tested almost every year — memorize this result.
String vs rod distinction is a classic conceptual question.
Tension at top and bottom problems are standard numerical questions.
Top minimum: v_top = √(gr) — just take √(g × r).
Bottom minimum (string): v_bottom = √(5gr) — remember the factor 5.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: The ideal banking angle tan θ = v²/(rg) is independent of vehicle mass.
At design speed, no friction is needed — the horizontal component of normal force provides all centripetal…
Banking with friction increases the maximum safe speed beyond the design speed.
Railway superelevation h = w tan θ applies the same physics to train tracks.
Over-banking (θ too large for the speed) causes inward sliding; under-banking causes outward skidding.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Ideal banking angle (no friction): tan θ = v²/(rg)
Maximum speed with friction: v_max = √[rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)]
Minimum speed with friction: v_min = √[rg(tan θ − μ)/(1 + μ tan θ)]
Railway superelevation: h = w tan θ, where w = track gauge
Normal force on banked road: N = mg/cos θ

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: The ideal banking angle is given by tan θ = v²/(rg), independent of the vehicle's mass.
On a banked road with friction, the maximum safe speed is v_max = √[rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)].
At the design speed, the horizontal component of the normal force alone provides the centripetal force.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: Deriving tan θ = v²/(rg) is the most common NEB question — know the force resolution steps.
Maximum speed with friction problems are standard numerical questions.
Railway superelevation: know h = w tan θ and that w ≈ 1.5 m for standard gauge.
Design speed shortcut: v = √(rg tan θ) — square root of rg times tangent of angle.
Friction-free shortcut: if the problem says 'no friction needed', use tan θ = v²/(rg).
